item.title: Farewell to Summer and Playing With Sand
item.description:
Child Development

Farewell to Summer and Playing With Sand

The psychology behind why sand is the perfect plaything for humans

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • Free play in sand can make way for free expression and symbolic, useful storytelling.
  • Sand play therapists take advantage of these stories.
  • Play is learning.

If you hit the beach this summer, you are likely to agree with the folklorist Jay Mechling, who proclaimed sand to be “the perfect plaything for humans.” He had good reason to think so.

For starters, sand feels good and inviting on bare feet. Especially so when it is warmed by the sun. Warm sand yields underfoot; strained through toes, it gives way to footprints that track the beginning of play. Molded and sloped and topped with a beach towel, sand makes for an improvised recliner. Playful engineering invites and enables relaxation and contemplation. There is a purpose to re-creation. Sand will drift, and at the beach, so will your mind.

Dry sand begs to be scooped, lifted, sifted, and streamed out idly through an almost closed fist. Dry sand, made up of minute solids, tiny broken bits of shell and stone, once loosed, behaves almost as a liquid. Sand flows beguilingly through toy plastic funnels. At the beach, gravity powers the dry fluid instructively through toy paddles and wheels.

Sand can be shoveled and ruffled and raked through without consequence. Sand is clean. Sand brushes off. Sand is not mud.

Parents may sink pennies into the sand, making up a story about a buried pirate hoard and launching a treasure hunt. Fancy metal detectors may hunt for stray earrings or lost items or fantasy doubloons if the searcher is in a storytelling mood. Because sand shapes can be so easily made, unmade, and remade, the medium encourages playful invention.

But wet sand yields even more easily to imaginative or impish play. A toe may trace a line in the wet sand, daring a companion to cross. With waves lapping, a stick may leave a temporary text—two names with a heart in the middle, “Beware sharks!” inscribed playfully on a Great Lakes beach, or for a modern postcard photo-op, “Wish you were here!”

A sunbathing sand-sculpture, artist unknown, found on Grand Traverse Bay.
Source: Image courtesy of Scott Eberle (2026)

Very wet sand can be dribbled. A sandcastle, its stout sand foundations laid with overturned buckets, and its walls scored with crenellations, will be decorated with dribbled parapets. Shells, if handy, will suffice for portcullises. Moats will protect the curtain walls. In saltwater environs, captured sand crabs may be recruited as temporary knights. But mutinously, they will quickly burrow away from their little human commanders.

Listen to kids as they construct with sand, their “sandwork,” as the folklorist calls it. They narrate. They tell stories. They will recruit the mythologies they know so well. Taking Transformers as inspiration, perhaps. Or the characters from the Pokémon universe that they know in such detail will fill out the unfolding folklore.

article continues after advertisement

I listened in recently to kids playing at building a sandcastle, but couldn’t keep up with the dizzying side yarn that a five-year-old and a seven-year-old together wove from an elaborately rule-bound pantheon of heroes. I heard something about Corpish and more about Kingler, who seemed to be something like crabs. They were stalwart guards at any rate, protecting the castle against—well, here I lost the thread.

Free association like this is never truly free, because it draws not just from the elaborate established lore—the origin stories and the deep well of the characters’ titanic, unceasing conflicts—but children also weave their feelings into their storytelling. Their stories trend.

It is a phenomenon, the children’s rolling, revealing creativity, that almost a century ago attracted the attention of psychotherapists and embroiled them in a fierce debate. To sum up. On the one side, Melanie Klein believed that young children’s play was equivalent to free association and opened therapy to children who could not otherwise describe their emotions. Impulses of anger and envy could thereby be analyzed and allayed. Anna Freud (Sigmund’s daughter) disagreed, believing that young children remained inaccessible because they lacked the mature adult ego that would open the subconscious to analysis.

A succeeding generation, Jungians this time, leapfrogged the impasse and made “sandplay therapy” a standard instrument in the diagnosis and treatment of children’s trauma. In the clinical setting, free, undirected play in sand fosters free expression and useful, symbolic storytelling. Toys in sand trays stand in for archetypes—heroes, sages, rulers, magicians, monsters, masked shadowy villains, and the rest. These, not coincidentally, map closely onto the Pokémon characters that populate and fuel children’s storytelling at the beach.

American Psychology and Sand Play

It happens that sand play also featured in the history of American psychology. One of its founding generation, G. Stanley Hall, the first to receive a doctorate in psychology in the United States and founder of the venerable American Journal of Psychology, wrote a slim volume, The Story of the Sand Pile, that speaks to us with such sustained good sense that the text deserves a contemporary read. (Hall also purveyed a steady stream of conventional late Victorian claptrap—racial eugenics, for example—but stick with me for his thoughts about sand play.)

In a summer retreat 30 miles outside Boston, a clever neighbor, meaning to occupy footloose neighborhood kids, arranged to have loads of “fine clean sand” delivered to his yard.

Sim City Before SimCity

Over the course of weeks and succeeding summers, these children built their own Lilliputian 3-D (and thus superior) version of SimCity. They transformed featureless piles with scraps of wood and twigs to make houses and barns, and they laid out a dozen mini-farms.

article continues after advertisement

In their intense, “bright focus of attention,” voluntary play elaborated and codified. The players organized and cooperated to solve problems, imagining systems of transportation, agriculture, governance, and a market economy. They stacked firewood and baled fodder. They built bridges. They promulgated laws overseeing public safety. (A firecracker had blown up a house…) They invented a currency. They diversified occupations. They improvised toy carts and improved designs.

Free Play Is Learning

Hall, tendentiously, saw in this play a recapitulation of the growth of civilization. But the less extravagant and more lasting lesson that he extracted from the summers with the sand pile holds today. Free, imaginative, non-adult-directed play is learning. Sand-pile players aged out at about 14. But in the interval before that, creativity and spontaneity reigned. “On the whole, the sand-pile has, in the opinion of the parents, as much educational value to the boys as eight months of school,” Hall wrote.

Play with the perfect plaything for humans paid an additional dividend, according to Hall: “the boys have become more companionable and rational.” Then as now in the sand. Play trends toward understanding.

item.title: Reflecting on My Aging Mother’s Move to a Retirement Home
item.description:
Aging

Reflecting on My Aging Mother’s Move to a Retirement Home

Getting old isn’t for wimps.

Posted August 21, 2026

In January, I wrote an article titled “Letting Go of Parents,”1 which tells my story about my attempt to emotionally “let go” of my 93-year-old mother. My grown children have prepared me for letting go through many implicit and overt messages, such as “This is not about you, mum.” The recent experiences with my mother have been different from and similar to those with my grown children. I recognise the see-saw.

I try to be there for my children and grandchildren as much as I can when I’m needed, which isn’t so much these days. At the same time, I find myself carefully opining, just a little, with my mother. Mum needs me physically and as an advocate for her. I am conscious of respecting her wishes and, foremost, to support her dignity. Of course, to add another layer, I’m thinking about how things will unfold for my husband and myself in our future.

Like my children, my mother is feisty, opinionated, and strong, with a sense of humor. Unlike them, her body and her mind often play tricks on her. They aren’t so reliable anymore. For the last six months, she has had to navigate this understanding together with the sadness and pain of losing her close companion of 15 years.

Fast forward to the last six weeks

There has been rapid change. Five weeks ago, when I was in Sydney for one of my visits, we experienced the serendipity of right timing.

I received an email that a vacancy had come up for mum for respite in a retirement home. I nearly discarded the email because, after discussing it ad nauseam, our agreed stance was that mum would stay in her own home until she knew she couldn't manage. In hindsight, this was fantasy. We were convincing ourselves and each other that this was ok, avoiding the reality and knowing that this situation was a ticking time bomb.

My gut feeling was to be totally transparent and read her the email without influencing her.

I don't know why I was surprised by her response. “Yes, I want to go.” Once again, she led the charge as her main caregiver, my brother, mum, and I, discussed this option face-to-face.

The next day, we went on a visit to the retirement home. She warmed to it. It was on the same street she lived on when she was first married to my father 68 years ago, and is only one mile from her current apartment.

She admitted that she no longer feels physically safe at home. Every night, she was barricading the front door against intruders. She was often confused, very lonely, and overwhelmed by running her household. Her only constant companion was the television, which she watched intently and inspired her politically incorrect commentary.

She knew her home was becoming too much, but she needed to come to that realization herself. The alternative to full-time care there was anathema to her, so when the opportunity for respite came, she grabbed it. We comforted ourselves that her apartment would always be available to return to if she wanted. We both knew her move would be challenging.

I came back for move-in day. She was happy and relieved. Her mantras comforted her. "I’ll make sure to be happy there." "I can’t stay alone anymore, I need to be looked after." "I’ve had a blessed life with two men who looked after me." "I have three loving children, and you need to live your lives without worrying about me."

article continues after advertisement

Leaving her home

This will remain with me forever. Mum was stoic and resourceful.

Of course, she was also fragile, disoriented, cranky, and sad when we arrived at her front door. “I can’t find my hearing aids. I have too many bags; they won’t let me in.” She was absorbing the reality that most likely this was the last time she would wake up in her home of almost 50 years, a home that was full of memories. But she closed the door and charged ahead.

Her arrival at the retirement home

"It’s so welcoming. So clean. Everyone is so lovely. The food is good. There are people there to talk to, and I have a lovely room to go to when I want to be alone.”

Over the past four days, she has demonstrated incredible wisdom, selflessness, humor, and presence of mind. She’s finding her feet. She played bridge yesterday, and she can even find the dining room.

An added bonus is that her sister is there. The familial banter and sibling rivalry are creeping in. They can’t always hear each other, but they are a hilarious duo. This will keep them both going. The sight of seeing them sitting together at lunch is so warming and comforting.

I have learnt so much from this experience

  • We don't give enough acknowledgment to the amazing physical and emotional feats that the elderly accomplish as they are forced to manage their decline. We need to celebrate their triumphs and what they can teach us. We might be there one day.
  • My mother is fortunate on so many levels. She is in relatively good emotional and physical health. She is flexible, smart, and has her faculties most of the time. As her body and mind deteriorate, her feeling antenna ascends; we need to remember this.
  • She is lucky to be in a place where she is cared for and respected. To the amazing staff, thank you. This piece is for mum and you.

I left her today to return to my family. When we hugged goodbye, Mum said she would miss me, and I replied: “I’ll miss you and I’ll be back in five weeks.” I added, “I have been your ears and eyes for the last four days, it's your turn now. You will be ok.”

I reminded her that G-d has decided for her to be 93.

In mum’s words: “Getting older isn’t for wimps.”

In the meantime, I’m planning her 94th birthday party for when I return to Sydney next month.

item.title: We Can Hold the Hard Things and Still Have Fun
item.description:
Resilience

We Can Hold the Hard Things and Still Have Fun

How small moments of joy, play, and laughter can help us carry what's hard.

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • Hard things and joy can coexist.
  • Small moments of lightness are part of what helps us keep going.
  • We can intentionally make more room for play, joy, and fun in our grown-up lives.

A dual truth I think many of us need a reminder of right now is that life can be hard and bumpy and the world may feel genuinely unwell, and there can still be a throughline of joy, play, and merriment running underneath it. Not instead of the hard, but alongside it.

We can acknowledge what is sad, scary, and difficult, and still make room for joy, play, laughter, and connection. Experiencing and creating moments of joy doesn’t mean we’re ignoring what’s hard. Sometimes, those moments are what help us carry it.

A Place for Play, Fun, and Joy

As children, we naturally gravitated towards play, often without any particular goal in mind. We reveled in the simple pleasure of it. Yet somewhere between childhood and adulthood, many of us stop playing.

As we transition into the world of work and adult responsibilities, we can reluctantly leave play behind, as societal norms and expectations suggest that everything in the “real world” is high-stakes and serious. We trade recess for productivity and tell ourselves this is simply the cost of being a grown-up. We can forget the power of silliness, the bright relief of laughter, or the comfort that comes from a shared moment of merriment because there’s always something else that needs our attention, another goal to reach, or another problem to solve.

These moments might just be what gives us a chance to breathe, reconnect with ourselves and others, and remind us there is still room for something good.

The Power of Fun

I recently had a conversation with Dave Raymond, the original Phillie Phanatic: the giant green mascot who has delighted Philadelphia sports fans for years. Dave brought the character to life for 16 years before moving into speaking and consulting on what he calls the power of fun.

Dave makes a distinction between “known fun” and “powerful fun” in his work. Known fun is the fun we all recognize and use for time off or vacation. Powerful fun is a different force. He describes powerful fun as “iterated, designed, and created specifically for the moment that you’re in” (Perspective Shift, 2026). It's intentional and purposeful.

This is the kind of fun that shows up in a hospital room during a family’s worst week. It’s the fun that walks into a funeral home, not to distract from grief but to sit alongside it. Dave described being invited into both settings in costume and being told afterward by grieving and hurting families that he had given them the best medicine they could have received. He didn’t understand it at the time, but he does now. Powerful fun doesn’t erase what’s painful, but it can make a small amount of room next to it.

I believe this matters for how we think about joy in our own lives. We often assume that if something is hard enough, fun becomes off-limits until the hard thing resolves. Dave’s experience, and a good body of research on adult play and resilience, suggests the opposite.

Research shows that playfulness can improve mood and contribute to stress coping and greater flexibility and resilience when faced with challenges (Chang et al., 2013; Magnuson & Barnett, 2013). The heavier the season, the more we may need those small, deliberate pockets of lightness.

article continues after advertisement

A Tick Above Where You Are

When you feel as though you’re stuck in the abyss, you don’t necessarily need a giant leap forward. Sometimes, you just need one small thing that offers a moment of relief, lightness, or hope. Dave called this a “finger hold,” borrowing the mountain-climbing image of the small ledge that lets you stay balanced before your next move. Something that gets you a fraction of an inch above where you are. It could be a favorite song, playing with your kids, watching something that makes you laugh, calling a friend, or returning to an activity you loved doing as a child.

For Dave, showing up in costume to bring a flicker of joy to strangers ended up giving something back to him too. It was a lifeline back to hope. Service and presence can move in both directions, creating a little light for them and for us, too.

So, what might it look like to make a little more room for play in our grown-up lives?

Practical Ways to Reclaim Joy and Play as Adults

  1. Reconnect with childhood passions and interests: What was something you could do for hours as a child? Whatever comes up for you may serve as a good indicator of what might feel playful and enjoyable for you today.
  2. Try something new: Seek out a new hobby or activity that might bring you joy and fulfillment. Give yourself permission to be a rookie at something new.
  3. Create a playful environment: Make it easier for play to happen. Keep playful tools and materials accessible. We tend to reach for what is available.
  4. Schedule time for play: If it is always something you’ll get to “when you have time,” it may never happen. Try putting a small block of play on your calendar and honor it as you would any important meeting.
  5. Get outside: Whatever happened to recess? Nature is our first playground. Spending time outside and reconnecting with the natural world can help us step away from our usual routines and make space for physical, cognitive, and emotional renewal.
  6. Try a playful pattern interrupt: Invite a little more play into the moment. Share a laugh, play a silly game, take a spontaneous side quest, or find another small way to shift the energy.

Final Thoughts

Fun doesn’t mean we’re ignoring what matters. Joy doesn’t mean we’re not taking something seriously. Play doesn’t mean we’ve stopped being productive. Making room for them may be part of how we keep going. Perhaps we can give ourselves permission to rediscover the joy of play for play’s sake and find small ways to let a little more light in.

article continues after advertisement

My gentle invitation is to ask yourself:

What was one small thing that made me smile or brought a moment of relief this week?

Who in my world helps me find silly or joyful moments, even for a breath?

Where can I interrupt my own weariness or heaviness with a playful pause?

When life feels hard, what’s one small thing that could make it feel a little lighter?

What’s a gesture that can lift someone else today?

We don’t have to choose between acknowledging what’s real and the weight of what's difficult, and making room for the things that bring us joy. We can hold both.

item.title: When Feeling Lost Is A Path Forward
item.description:
Resilience

When Feeling Lost Is A Path Forward

What uncertainty can teach us about finding our way.

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • Feeling lost isn’t a failure. Sometimes it’s a sign that you’re in motion.
  • You don’t need a perfect map. Sometimes clarity comes after you take the first step.
  • You’re not behind or off track. You may simply be finding your way back to yourself.
Source: Andrew Neel / Unsplash

There are seasons in life when the path ahead feels clear, and others when you have no idea where you’re going. This excerpt from Notes on Hope is for anyone who happens to be in one of those more uncertain chapters right now. It’s a reminder that if you’re feeling a little lost, perhaps you don’t need to find your way just yet.

Why Feeling Lost is Part of Growth

There will be chapters in your life when you don’t know where you’re going. The map is blurry, the path is uncertain, and every direction feels equally possible and impossible. Feeling lost isn’t a failure—it’s a sign that you’re in motion, even if it doesn’t feel like it yet. You’re in the process of evolving, of shedding one version of yourself before fully stepping into the next. You’re in the process of getting lost in order to find your way.

Detours that feel like mistakes are often your biggest teachers. They slow you down, they reroute you, and they throw questions at you that you didn’t know you needed to answer. They make you journey inward and ask: What do I truly want? Who am I becoming? What still feels right for me? What now feels wrong? This is healthy. This is human. This is how growth happens.

If you don’t know where you’re going next, you don’t have to rush. Stand still for a moment. Breathe. Let the dust settle. Stillness is not stagnation; it’s information. It’s your inner compass recalibrating. Sometimes the wisest thing you can do is simply wait until something inside you whispers: Now.

And when you do feel ready to move, take just one small step. Any step, in any direction. You don’t need a five-year plan or a flawless map. A single step will give you feedback. Listen to it. If it feels expansive, take another. If it feels heavy or wrong, pause. Adjust. Begin again. There is no rush. Your pace is your truth.

One of the most liberating things you can learn is that clarity often comes after the step, not before it. Sometimes you have to wander a little to realize what home feels like. Sometimes you might not know where you’re going until you’ve arrived. Trust the process. Trust yourself. Trust the universe; she has a way of guiding those who are willing to listen with an open heart.

Progress via Small, Continuous Steps

Someone once said to me, “I want to move forward, but I don’t know how.” I said, “Begin with one tiny step. Then take another. Without realizing it, you’re already moving forward.” This applies just as much literally as metaphorically. Progress doesn’t always feel like a breakthrough. Sometimes it’s tiny steps you barely notice. Other times it’s just a soft shift inside you. Sometimes it’s simply a willingness to keep going.

I often think of Alice before she reached Wonderland. She had to fall first. She had to tumble through confusion, uncertainty, and unfamiliarity. Maybe we’re all Alices in our own ways, falling and spiraling, not entirely sure where we’ll land. But maybe your version of Wonderland is closer than you think: a place where kindness guides you, hope steadies you, and a slower, more mindful pace begins to feel natural. A place where healing happens, where transformation settles in, where the Earth beneath your feet feels like home again.

article continues after advertisement

Being lost really isn’t the opposite of being found. It’s the doorway to it. These are the places where hope often shows up; the places you never planned to go and the unexpected detours you didn’t see coming. These are the places that lead you back to yourself.

You’re not off track. You’re not behind. You’re not running out of time. You’re simply in a chapter where the path is revealing itself step by step, breath by breath.

Wander bravely. Listen deeply. Let the unknown shape you rather than scare you. And, most of all, keep journeying forward.

Journaling Prompt

Think of a time in your life when you felt lost. What did that chapter reveal about you?

Be brave with your answers.

This essay is an excerpt from the author’s book, Notes on Hope.

item.title: Can’t Get Along? Try Rejecting Free Will
item.description:
Persuasion

Can’t Get Along? Try Rejecting Free Will

A new approach to building trust and bridging our divides.

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • Facts and figures often fail to convince someone on the opposing side.
  • Accepting that free will is an illusion resets the conversation.
  • No one freely became who they are, but we can influence who they become.
  • Persuasion is a marathon that is won by building trust and understanding.

If it seems that Americans are more polarized than ever, eagerly segregating into “us versus them” camps on every issue, it’s not your imagination. Polls suggest that Americans are creating divides amongst themselves faster than other nations, which threatens national security and well-being.

What hope is there for civil democracy when we are so fervently divided that the impetus to understand one another evaporates? How can you have a constructive conversation with people who directly oppose your values or deny the facts as you see them?

As a scientist who engages in public outreach, I frequently encounter skeptics of topics like climate change, vaccines, and evolution. My responses used to be counterattacks, drawing on an arsenal of facts and figures. As my fellow science communicators will admit with befuddlement, this strategy often fails, especially on topics that have become politically charged. How do you break through to someone so divorced from the reality you know?

No one forms their beliefs in a vacuum

When science skeptics scoff at attempts to rectify a knowledge deficit, we conclude they are being willfully ignorant and disengage. This unproductive response ignores mounting evidence that free will is an illusion. Invisible forces beyond our control shape personality, behavior, and beliefs. We don’t pick our genes. We had no say in our prenatal or childhood environment. We do not choose the culture, religion, or ideology that gets etched into our psyche during our formative years.

We can certainly change our minds, but that too is contingent on experiences that befall us: who we encounter, what we’re taught, whether trauma or privilege alters our path.

Life feels like a choice, but it seems we’re behind the wheel of a self-driving car. While interpretations are debated, neurobiologists have established that subconscious brain activity occurs before we are conscious of our intention to perform simple tasks.

Even when we consciously deliberate on a decision, we have no control over the thoughts that bubble up from the dark cauldron of our subconscious. Furthermore, the judgment we cast upon each of those thoughts is anchored by a causal chain of prior events.

As it is now generally agreed that biological and environmental forces greatly constrain beliefs and behavior, admonishing someone for being willfully ignorant feels like a hypocritical copout. Instead, we should embrace our lack of agency to engender more fruitful interactions with people who believe and do things that bewilder us.

Rejecting agency resets your relationship

Imagine you’re having an uncomfortable encounter with someone who doesn’t see things your way. You can marshal evidence and masterfully rebut every dubious claim, but these approaches are shockingly ineffective because we view reality through different lenses. A lifetime of unique experiences dictates who we trust and what we perceive as factual.

article continues after advertisement

The 2015 dress meme demonstrates how people can view the same image differently. Whether someone sees the dress as blue and black or white and gold depends on how their visual system unconsciously perceives the lighting, a physiological property beyond our command. If you could see the dress through another person’s eyes, you would agree with the colors they see.

It’s the same for worldviews. What we believe to be reality has been filtered through a lens we had no hand in grinding. When confronted with opposition, remember that if you had their genes and life experiences, you would see the world as they do. They cannot help who they are any more than you can help who you are.

This does not mean that it’s pointless to try to change someone’s beliefs. You can become a voice in their mind’s choir. Your words may season their subconscious soup, nudging them towards rethinking their position.

Acknowledging that people have little to no free will can help affect change in another person. When we accept that someone has no control over who they are, we can shift our focus from persuasion to understanding. Stop being the arbiter of truth and become a curious interviewer.

What led this person to feel what they feel, trust who they trust, and believe what they believe? The answers will steer the dialogue from an angry sea to deeper, calmer waters. You’ll learn what this person values, which can help reframe your position to break through their resistance more than charts and graphs ever will.

Change the objective of the conversation

When you ask nonjudgmental questions with a genuine desire to learn rather than contest, you gain an appreciation of other perspectives. You’re also prompting them to inspect their own lens, potentially leading them to see the smudges and cracks in their vision of the world without being confrontational. When asked to provide detailed explanations of our beliefs, it often exposes information gaps or inconsistencies with our values.

article continues after advertisement

Sharing your different life stories makes for a more interesting conversation than the predictable exchange of dogmatic talking points that defend our respective positions. An individual’s personal history is fascinating, and the story underlying their worldview may surprise you. It’s not always a knowledge deficit or misinformation, but a difference in values, what we fear, and who we trust, often stemming from an emotive experience.

This is why it is crucial to have a congenial conversation that uncovers things you have in common. Seize upon those similarities. They lighten the weight of the differences. They are planks that build a bridge connecting your worlds. Dr. Daryl Davis illustrates the power of this approach, which he employs to get Ku Klux Klan members to renounce their racism.

Recognizing that those unlike you reached their position because life steered them down a different path fosters a more compassionate encounter that mends trust and provides opportunities to learn from one another. The first step to opening the door to someone’s mind is to convince them that you can be trusted with the key.

Winning an argument is a marathon, and you’ll never win minds without winning hearts.
